text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHealthHow the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s DiseaseBoring jobs are important jobsJCBy Jake Currie7:00 AM CST on November 12, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIt seems like every other day a new report comes out linking another gene variant to Alzheimer’s disease. Powered By 1085.3K 40ShareNextStayCASS4, a member of a family of scaffold genes, is one of these genes. As far as genes go, its function seems fairly mundane. It codes for a protein involved in intracellular infrastructure and adhesion. However, several studies have tied single nucleotide polymorphisms in CASS4 to an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s. Now a new study published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine is helping explain why. “Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease,” study author Addie Walsh of the University of Virginia explained in a statement. “Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper.”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
